brief.notification_title: Anthropic lifts futures; hawkish Fed still sets the tone
brief.market_summary: US futures are bouncing after five straight S&P 500 declines: ES 7,412.50 (+0.98%) and NQ 27,663 (+1.75%), helped by Anthropic pricing its record $107.3B IPO at $83 and by Palo Alto's beat-and-raise. Underneath, the Fed backdrop got more hawkish: the minutes showed "almost all" officials expect more hikes, a 50bp move was discussed, and about 92% of a December 25bp hike is priced. Still, the 10Y moved only +1.2bp to 5.078% while growth data softened (Philly Fed 6.3 vs ~20, permits and pending home sales missed, GDPNow down to 3.2%). Brent is down to $90.03 (-2.1%, -17% over a month) on a 3.4M-barrel EIA build and surplus forecasts. Bitcoin is stuck near $63.9K after $306.5M of ETF outflows.
brief.since_last: 1) Fed minutes (Wed 14:00 ET) were hawkish. "Almost all" officials saw further hikes as likely (n67), a 50bp December move was discussed (n177), and Waller backs a bigger hike (n87). JPMorgan now forecasts three hikes through March 2027 (n92). The long end shrugged it off: 10Y 5.078% (+1.2bp), TLT +0.84% Wednesday, and the 20Y auction cleared at 5.459% vs 5.469% last time. 2) Anthropic priced at $83 and raised $107.3B (n18). It indicated about 25% above the IPO price on Hyperliquid before its debut (n31), and Nasdaq futures are up about 2%. 3) Earnings: PANW beat and raised guidance (up 7–10% pre-market); WMT beat and raised its full-year EPS guide to $2.84–2.89; BABA beat on revenue but missed on EPS. 4) Thursday data was soft on growth: claims 203K vs ~198K; Philly Fed 6.3 vs ~20, though prices paid jumped to 58.2 from 43.2. 5) Brent fell from about $92 in Asia to $90.03 despite Hormuz mine reports. 6) Nvidia's interim CEO Kress held her first all-hands since Jensen Huang's exit (n83). Data caveat: the economic calendar stamps the housing, EIA, 20Y auction and TIC items "19 Nov GMT", and some of those times haven't arrived yet. Because they carry actuals and match the usual Wednesday schedule, I treat them as already released, but the timestamps are unreliable.

economic_data.takeaway: Slightly above consensus and still historically low; the 4-week average is 197.75K and continuing claims 1.763M. It doesn't change the December hike pricing, but it adds to a softening trend in the data.

A large growth miss, but prices paid jumped to 58.2 from 43.2. That stagflationary mix explains why yields haven't fallen on it: growth is slowing, yet the Fed's inflation concern gets support. The growth side supports a duration starter; the prices side argues against chasing it.

Permits, the forward-looking series, missed badly. Together with NAHB at 25 (vs 29 expected), MBA 30Y mortgage rates at 7.35% and pending home sales at -4.7% (vs -2.0% expected), housing is buckling under 5%+ long rates. That is the transmission channel the Fed is counting on.
The consumer is still spending; the control group beat. It fits the TGT, LOW and WMT beats and gives the Fed cover to keep hiking.
Weak headline, but manufacturing output rose 0.3% (vs 0.2% expected), so the drag came from outside factories. Capacity utilization slipped to 76.4%.

A second straight large build, after API showed +5.3M. Gasoline stocks swelled too. This supports the IEA surplus view and is why Brent can't hold rallies on Hormuz headlines. Cushing drew 1.2M, a small offset for WTI.
It cleared slightly below the prior auction's yield despite the hawkish minutes the same afternoon, so long-end demand is holding at these levels.
Still solid, but revisions are now pointing down. A falling nowcast while the Fed signals more hikes is the setup where the long end starts to price policy overtightening.

The 1-yr inflation expectation (previous 4.3%) matters more than the headline. A print at or below 4.3% triggers the second IEF tranche. A clear rise would back the 50bp camp and push the front end higher.

sections.summary: The S&P 500 closed at 7,323.63 (-0.23%), its fifth straight decline. The Dow fell 1.11% while the Nasdaq rose 0.42%, and the index is down 3.9% over the week. Futures are bouncing (ES +0.98%, NQ +1.75%) on Anthropic's $83 IPO pricing, PANW's beat and a memory-chip rebound. The macro anchor hasn't moved, though: the 10Y is above 5%, the dollar is near a 19-month high (n114) and the Fed is hiking. I'd treat this as a liquidity-event bounce until semis confirm it.
key_points: Anthropic priced at $83 and raised a record $107.3B (n18); it indicated about 25% above the IPO price on Hyperliquid before the open (n31). Alphabet and Amazon are up in sympathy (n11).
SMH is at 459.54, down 9.4% in a week and 15.9% in a month. Memory names (MU, SNDK, Intel) are rebounding pre-market (n29, n89), and Nvidia now has an interim CEO (n83).
VIX is 22.62, down 7.9% today but up 35.6% over the month. Wednesday's sector spread: XLY +1.79% (retail beats) vs XLE -3.27% and XLV -2.20%.
XLP and XLU are each up about 4% over the month while XLK is down 11.7%; the shift into defensives is stretched (n90).

sections.summary: The minutes were about as hawkish as they could be: 'almost all' officials expect more hikes, 50bp was discussed, and a 25bp hike in December is about 92% priced. Even so, the 10Y rose only 1.2bp to 5.078% and the 20Y auction cleared below its last yield. Growth data are softening (Philly 6.3, permits -7.4%, GDPNow 3.2%), so the long end is starting to look past the hikes. Bills still pay 4.15% for no duration risk.
key_points: Yields: 13-week 4.150%, 5Y 4.902%, 10Y 5.078%, 30Y 5.420%. Over the past month the 5Y is down 7.0bp, the 10Y down 6.8bp and the 30Y down only 1.9bp.
IEF closed at 90.67 and TLT gained 0.84% Wednesday. In credit, LQD rose 0.40% and HYG was flat (+0.03%), so high yield isn't joining the rally.
JPMorgan sees three hikes through March 2027 (n92). Kashkari says the market expects more hikes than officials do (n171), a small dovish counterweight.
Foreign buying of T-bonds slowed to $80.8B from $108.6B (TIC). Today's bill auctions: $115B of 4-week and $110B of 8-week.

EIA showed a 3.4M-barrel crude build (vs +0.4M expected) and a 5.2M gasoline build, the IEA sees a surplus through 2027, and Gulf exports are near pre-war levels. WTI is oddly flat at $83.37 (+0.13%), so read today's Brent move with some caution.

brief.instructor_take: The futures rally is about one stock's debut, not about the economy, and I wouldn't let it pull you into risk. Here's what I see. The Fed told us on Wednesday that almost everyone expects more hikes and some want 50bp, yet the 10Y rose barely a basis point and long-end auction demand held. When the bond market shrugs at hawkish news, it's usually saying the hikes will slow growth, and this week's data back that up: Philly Fed collapsed to 6.3, permits fell 7.4%, pending home sales dropped 4.7% and GDPNow is slipping. What a less experienced investor might miss is the other half of the Philly report: prices paid jumped to 58.2. The Fed can't pivot on growth alone while that is happening, which is why I'm building duration slowly instead of all at once. On equities, a $107.3B IPO is a supply event. It pulls cash out of other holdings (look at the BTC ETF outflows), and a day-one pop says little about the next month. Semis are down 16% in a month after a huge Nvidia beat, with a leadership change on top, so I want price to confirm before I buy anything there. So I'd keep the T-bill sleeve as the core, hold the IEF starter, and stay out of oil and crypto. I'll change my mind if the 10Y breaks above 5.30% or if SMH reclaims $500.

top_ideas.title: T-bill sleeve stays the core while the Fed hikes
top_ideas.one_liner: 4.15% bills, no duration risk, and dry powder for the next dip
top_ideas.thesis: The Fed is still hiking: December is about 92% priced and the minutes discussed 50bp. That keeps bill yields rising (13-week now 4.150%, up 8.7bp in a month). SGOV earns that carry with almost no price risk and funds ideas 2 and 3 if their triggers hit.
top_ideas.reasoning: I start from the policy path. When nearly every FOMC member expects more hikes, the front end is the only part of the curve that benefits directly, because bills reset higher at each auction. The 13-week bill moved from 4.143% to 4.150% since yesterday, and JPMorgan's three-hike call (n92) suggests there's further to go. I prefer this to a money-market sweep or longer bonds because it keeps price risk near zero. The concept is the opportunity cost of cash: it's low today, because cash pays above 4% while equities and crypto are still going through price discovery. This is also where you wait out a VIX at 22 without having to guess. I'll be wrong if the Fed starts talking about ending hikes after December, or if the 13-week falls below 4.0% because markets start pricing cuts. Today's soft Philly print is an early version of that risk, but one print isn't a trend.
catalysts: Fri 20 Nov 10:00 ET: UoM inflation expectations
risks: Growth breaks faster than expected and the market starts pricing cuts, so bill yields fall
Opportunity cost if the Anthropic-led bounce turns into a sustained rally
top_ideas.entry: Keep the existing position and add idle cash at market today. This sleeve funds the IEF second tranche and any later SMH rebuild.
top_ideas.invalidation: The 13-week yield (now 4.150%) falls below 4.0%, or Fed speakers signal the hiking cycle ends in December.
top_ideas.sizing: Core cash sleeve; 20–30% of the portfolio is reasonable for this backdrop

top_ideas.title: Hold IEF starter; add second half only on trigger
top_ideas.one_liner: Long end ignored hawkish minutes; add on 5.20% 10Y or soft UoM
top_ideas.thesis: The first half was triggered after Wednesday's minutes (10Y about 5.06–5.08%, IEF about 90.67). Softening growth (Philly 6.3, permits -7.4%, GDPNow 3.2%) against a Fed still hiking is the classic setup for intermediate yields to peak. I'd add the second half only on better price or confirmation from inflation expectations.
top_ideas.reasoning: My evidence is how the market reacted, not what the Fed said. The minutes were as hawkish as could be expected, yet the 10Y rose just 1.2bp, TLT gained 0.84% Wednesday and the 20Y auction cleared below its prior yield. That pattern tells me the long end thinks the Fed will overtighten into a slowdown. The concept is that hikes eventually flatten and then lower longer yields once growth rolls over, and housing (NAHB 25, mortgages at 7.35%) shows the transmission is working. IEF's roughly 7-year duration gives me about 7% upside per 100bp of yield decline without TLT's volatility. I'm not adding the second half today, because Philly prices paid jumped to 58.2. If Friday's UoM 1-yr expectations also rise, the 50bp camp wins and yields could test 5.20–5.30%. That's why I'd scale in on either a better price or confirmation, not on hope. I'm wrong if the 10Y closes above 5.30%.
catalysts: Fri 20 Nov 10:00 ET: UoM 1-yr inflation expectations (previous 4.3%)
Next week's data and Fed speakers before the December FOMC
risks: Inflation expectations re-accelerate (Philly prices paid at 58.2) and the Fed delivers 50bp
Weaker foreign demand (TIC T-bond buying fell to $80.8B from $108.6B) lifts term premium
Oil rebounds sharply on an Iran strike and revives inflation fears
top_ideas.entry: Hold the first half (1–1.5% of the portfolio, bought around IEF 90.67). Buy the second half (1–1.5%) from SGOV if the 10Y backs up to 5.20–5.25% (IEF roughly 89.7–90.0), or on Friday if UoM 1-yr inflation expectations print at or below 4.3%. Don't add on today's soft Philly headline alone.
top_ideas.invalidation: A 10Y close above 5.30% (IEF near $89), or UoM 1-yr expectations clearly above 4.3% combined with Fed speakers endorsing 50bp.
top_ideas.sizing: 2–3% total in two halves, funded from SGOV

top_ideas.title: Don't chase the Anthropic pop into semis
top_ideas.one_liner: SMH -16% in a month; let it reclaim $500 before rebuilding
top_ideas.thesis: SMH is at 459.54, down 15.9% over the month, after Nvidia's beat failed to lift the price, and Nvidia now has an interim CEO. Today's bounce comes from a one-off IPO and memory-name short covering, not from a change in the rate backdrop. Keep the existing rebuild rules and don't buy ANT at the open either.
top_ideas.reasoning: The lesson from last week still holds: when a sector leader posts blowout numbers and the stock falls anyway, the market is telling you positioning was full, and that takes weeks to clear. Nothing in the overnight news changes that. The rally is driven by Anthropic's $107.3B raise and a rebound in memory names (n29, n89), while real yields above 5% still weigh on long-duration growth valuations. A record IPO also draws money away from existing AI holdings as funds make room, which can cap the rest of the group. Day-one IPO buyers, meanwhile, pay a scarcity premium (about 25% indicated over $83 on Hyperliquid) with no trading history to anchor it. I'd rather pay up after the market proves the bottom, with two closes above $500 (about 9% higher), than try to catch it. If KEYS tonight, HPE on 23 Nov and Dell on 24 Nov all beat and get rewarded, I'll rebuild on the rules below. If PANW-style software strength continues instead, the AI money is rotating within tech rather than leaving it.
catalysts: Today: Anthropic Nasdaq debut; KEYS and INTU after the close
Marvell reports around 26 Nov (verify the date; 26 Nov is US Thanksgiving)
risks: A violent short-covering rally in semis led by memory names leaves you under-exposed
A strong ANT debut re-rates the whole AI complex
Tech looks cheap against defensives (n90), and value buyers step in
top_ideas.entry: No new semis buying through ANT's first week. If SMH closes above $500 on two straight sessions, buy half the previously trimmed amount from SGOV. Buy the second half after ANT has traded a full week with SMH still above $500.
top_ideas.invalidation: Two consecutive SMH closes above $500 end the avoid. If SMH breaks to new lows after HPE and Dell, extend the avoid into December.
top_ideas.sizing: 0% new exposure; leave any residual core semis holding as is

brief.prior_ideas_review: 1) ADD SGOV: working as designed. The 13-week bill rose from 4.143% to 4.150%, and the minutes pointed to more hikes, not fewer, so neither invalidation is close. Keep. 2) BUY IEF: the first-half condition was met after Wednesday's 14:00 ET minutes, with the 10Y around 5.06–5.08%, well under the 5.15% cap. IEF closed at 90.67 against 90.66 at the last brief, so it's flat. The second half hasn't triggered: the 10Y is at 5.078%, not 5.20–5.25%, and the UoM test comes Friday. Keep with the same triggers, but don't add early given the jump in Philly prices paid. 3) AVOID SMH: correct so far. SMH is at 459.54 (-0.12% Wednesday, -9.4% for the week), far from the $500 rebuild level, and Nvidia's CEO change adds uncertainty. Keep through ANT's first week and reassess after HPE and Dell.

lesson.concept: Equity supply and the IPO pop
lesson.explanation: A big IPO is new supply: buyers have to sell something else, or use cash they'd otherwise spend elsewhere, to fund it. Day-one pops mostly reflect how scarce the allocation was, since many buyers got less than they wanted and chase in the open market. They say little about fair value over the following months. Record raises can lift sentiment for a day while draining money from the stocks and assets that investors sell to pay for the new shares.
lesson.todays_example: Anthropic raised $107.3B at $83 (n18) and indicated about 25% higher on Hyperliquid before trading (n31), lifting Nasdaq futures 1.75%. Meanwhile bitcoin ETFs saw $306.5M of outflows that CoinDesk ties partly to waning appetite before the debut (n69), and brokers are warning about flipping penalties (n30). That's a sign that allocations, not fundamentals, are driving the first trades.
